newsitem.title: USA: Dollar off against yen ahead of Japan, US trade data.
newsitem.headline: Dollar off against yen ahead of Japan, US trade data.

text.p: The dollar took little direction from U.S. economic data Tuesday, drifting mostly lower in advance of reports on Japanese and U.S. trade data and a gathering of world leaders later this week.

Government reports Tuesday showed the economy continues to grow at a healthy clip but is not generating enough inflation to prompt speculation that the Federal Reserve might move to raise interest rates, a development that would ordinarily strengthen the dollar.
A 0.1 percent rise in May consumer prices led a string of releases. Other data from May showed a 4.8 percent fall in the rate of new home starts and a 0.4 percent rise in factory output.

"It's just the sort of thing to keep the Fed happy," said Dennis Pettit, foreign exchange manager at Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan in New York. "We were not too excited one way or the other -- the big focus is on tonight's Japanese trade numbers and on Thursday's U.S. numbers."
The dollar ended at 1.7305 marks, off from 1.7315 and 113.32 yen, off from 113.43.
During New York trade, the dollar backed off its overnight highs. The yen in particular got some support as the market braced for the release of May data on Japanese trade early Wednesday.

The Japanese numbers seemed to take on added weight this time around. They immediately precede Thursday's Commerce Department report on the April U.S. trade deficit and the three-day gathering of leaders from the Group of Seven (G7) industrial nations -- Germany, France, Italy, Japan, Canada, Italy and the United States -- in Denver starting Friday.

"We had a big 174 percent jump in Japan's trade surplus with the U.S. last month and that's really kind of added some urgency to (Treasury Secretary Robert) Rubin asking for Japan to address it's external balance," said Keith Woodfin, an analyst at consulting firm Foreign Exchange Analytics.
Japan's trade surplus has ballooned recently, in part because the dollar's strength against the yen this year has made U.S. products more expensive and helped lift Japan's exports.
President Clinton is expected to zero in on Japan's trade surplus when he sits down with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto in Denver, a U.S. Treasury official said Tuesday.

The dollar was pressured by the report that Clinton and Hashimoto would have a one-on-one meeting at which Clinton was expected to stress Japan should not allow its trade surplus to rise substantially, Pettit said.
Elsewhere, the dollar rose to 1.4447 Swiss francs from 1.4425 Swiss francs and fell to Canadian $1.3865 from C$1.3872. The pound rose to $1.6393 from $1.6375.
